definition: AI computing capacity that a country builds or controls inside its borders, usually through a state-linked company, telecom operator or local cloud, so that data, models and capacity stay under national control. NVIDIA reports it as a demand category, not a segment.
NVIDIA's free membership program for start-ups (launched 2016). Members get technical help, training and introductions to investors and partners; NVIDIA takes no equity through the program.
NVIDIA's venture-capital arm, which buys minority equity in start-up funding rounds. It is separate from Inception (free membership) and from the large strategic stakes NVIDIA holds directly.
Minority equity investments made by an operating company in start-ups, usually for strategic information and ecosystem influence as well as financial return.
NVIDIA's GPU Technology Conference. The spring event in San Jose (first held in 2009) is NVIDIA's main roadmap keynote and partner launch window; regional editions run elsewhere during the year.
NVIDIA's training arm (DLI), which runs paid and free courses, instructor-led workshops and certifications on GPU programming and AI, often through universities and partners.

The programs a platform company runs to win and keep software developers: free tools and libraries, documentation, training, conferences and support. For NVIDIA it builds the CUDA habit that raises customers' switching costs.
A large IT services firm (for example Accenture) that designs, builds and runs technology projects for enterprises. GSIs decide much of what hardware and software a client deploys.
A company that resells, integrates or services a vendor's products, such as an OEM, distributor or systems integrator, letting the vendor reach customers without its own large sales force.

In NVIDIA's filings a direct customer buys from NVIDIA (mostly OEMs and ODMs); an indirect customer, such as a cloud provider or AI lab, buys the finished systems from them. NVIDIA discloses direct customers above 10% of revenue and estimates large indirect ones.
The share of revenue that comes from a few large customers. High concentration gives those buyers bargaining power and makes revenue sensitive to any one of them changing suppliers.
NVIDIA's licensed, supported software suite for running AI in companies (frameworks, NIM microservices, management tools), priced per GPU per year or per GPU-hour in the cloud.
NVIDIA Inference Microservices: pre-packaged containers that serve a specific AI model with NVIDIA's optimised runtime behind a standard API, sold as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise.

A vendor-specified, tested bill of materials and configuration (servers, network, storage, software) that partners can quote and support as a complete system. NVIDIA's enterprise version is called a validated design.
An air-cooled x86 server with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, sold by OEMs from 2025 for enterprises that cannot host liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.
Government rules that require a licence to sell certain technologies abroad. US rules on advanced GPUs decide which countries and buyers can receive NVIDIA's top chips and in what volume.
A non-binding document setting out the intended terms of a deal before definitive agreements are signed. NVIDIA's up-to-$100B OpenAI LOI (2025) was later replaced by a smaller equity investment.
A promise to buy any capacity a customer cannot sell to others, which lowers the customer's financing risk. NVIDIA agreed to buy up to $6.3B of CoreWeave's unsold capacity through 2032.
Stakes in private companies, carried at cost and re-measured only when an observable transaction (such as a new funding round) occurs. NVIDIA's OpenAI stake sits here.
Revaluing an asset at its current market price each reporting period. For NVIDIA's listed stakes, price changes flow into other income and can swing reported earnings.
Running AI workloads and radio-network signal processing on the same accelerated servers at mobile base stations. NVIDIA's $1B Nokia stake targets this market.
